tagline.text: Pablo Antonio's Art Deco architecture in Manila's university belt

location.label: Location
location.text: N. Reyes Street and Quezon Boulevard, Sampaloc, Manila (Far Eastern University)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~500 (transport and snacks, per person; admission and tour fees to be confirmed separately)

children.text: The FEU Manila campus is one of the largest surviving ensembles of Art Deco buildings in Manila, designed by Pablo Antonio between 1939 and 1950. Six of its buildings are National Cultural Treasures, and you can also see works by National Artists such as Botong Francisco and Vicente Manansala.

Far Eastern University (FEU) stands in Sampaloc, Manila, in the area commonly called the University Belt. The streets outside are packed with students, review centers and snack stalls, but the mood changes as soon as you step through the gate. Across a campus of about 4 to 5 hectares (figures vary by source), symmetrical buildings open onto a grassy central quadrangle, and many visitors describe it as an oasis in the middle of the city.

FEU began in 1928 as an accountancy institute founded by Nicanor Reyes Sr. (together with Francisco Dalupan Sr. and other educators). It merged with Far Eastern College in November 1933 and is generally said to have become a university in 1934. It reportedly first occupied a converted tobacco factory, which was demolished when the road was widened, and the school was rebuilt on its present site. From then on, the National Artist for Architecture Pablo Antonio designed the campus. Many of the reliefs and murals on the buildings form series on scenes from Philippine history, such as the Spanish, Chinese, American and industrial eras, so you can tour the campus almost like a gallery as well as an architecture site.

From the late 1930s until 1950, Antonio built Nicanor Reyes Hall, the Administration Building, the Admissions Building, the Architecture and Fine Arts Building and the Science Building, one after another. They are in the Art Deco style, marked by straight lines, symmetry and geometric ornament. In 2005 UNESCO's Asia-Pacific Heritage Awards gave the university an Honorable Mention for conserving the largest ensemble of Art Deco architecture that survives in Manila. In 2018 six of the buildings were declared National Cultural Treasures.

Between the buildings you will find paintings and sculptures by National Artists including Botong Francisco, Vicente Manansala and Napoleon Abueva. This is not a ticketed attraction but a working university where classes are still held, so the best way to enjoy it is to look around without disturbing students' daily routine.
Known as the oldest Art Deco building on campus, it was completed in

. The vertical lines and geometric ornament on the Quezon Boulevard facade are striking, and today it houses the university library and offices. Its third floor has been described as a viewpoint over the campus buildings, but check on site whether it is open to visitors.

Inside the Administration Building is an Art Deco theater designed around 1949 and restored in 2002–2003. Sources give its capacity as roughly 1,040 to 1,100 seats, and it was called the country's first fully air-conditioned auditorium. The lobby of the building has wooden reliefs by Francesco Monti and an Art Deco mural by Simon Saulog.

blocks.title: Architecture and Fine Arts Building and Science Building

children.text: The Architecture and Fine Arts (IARFA) Building went up in 1941, and the Science Building, Antonio's last campus design, was built in 1950. Seen side by side, they show how the same architect refined his style over a decade.

blocks.title: FEU Chapel and Botong Francisco's paintings

children.text: Designed by Felipe Mendoza, the chapel opened on December 8, 1957. Near the altar are the National Artist Botong Francisco's paintings of the Crucified Christ and the Stations of the Cross. It is a small space for about 300 people and serves as a prayer room for all faiths. Please stay quiet while services and prayers are going on.

In the right aisle of the chapel is Napoleon Abueva's fiberglass Pietà, and on the front is a mosaic by Vicente Manansala. Both are National Artists, so you can see their works together in one small chapel.

In the central quadrangle stands a Cubist sculpture by Manansala, whose copper has turned from gold to green over the years. In front of the Education Building is Tamalito, a bronze statue resembling the school mascot, the tamaraw (a small wild buffalo). It was unveiled on October 1, 2012, and is a favorite photo spot for students and visitors.

blocks.title: Art Deco heritage exhibition at the library

children.text: The university library has hosted an Art Deco heritage exhibition showing Pablo Antonio's drawings and photographs, and the university's student news outlet reported that it would run until February 2029, though the article shows no publication year and this could not be confirmed elsewhere. Before you go, it is safest to ask the university whether it is still on and when it can be viewed.

blocks.title: The Sarimanok and the marble floor, among other hidden details

children.text: The Administration Building and nearby buildings have Sarimanok (a legendary bird from Mindanao) works by Antonio Dumlao, some reportedly made partly from beer-bottle glass. The lobby floor is said to be laid with Carrara marble from Italy. These details are easy to miss without a guide's explanation, so ask about them when you inquire about a tour.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Seeing the Art Deco buildings and artworks

children.text: Before your visit, email FEU (info@feu.edu.ph) or contact the FEU Guides group on Facebook to ask about tours and how visitors are admitted. At the gate, tell the guard the purpose of your visit and follow his instructions.
Start by viewing the exterior of Nicanor Reyes Hall from Quezon Boulevard. Take your time with the symmetrical structure and the vertical ornament.
Enter the central quadrangle and look at Manansala's sculpture, then the facades of the Administration, Architecture and Fine Arts, and Science Buildings in turn.
See Monti's reliefs and Saulog's mural in the Administration Building lobby, and check the auditorium entrance as far as you are permitted.
Move to the chapel and quietly appreciate Botong Francisco's paintings and Abueva's Pietà.
Take photos at the Tamalito bronze in front of the Education Building, then have lunch at a restaurant near the university.
If you have time, look again at the library exhibition and the building exteriors, and rest in the shaded quadrangle during the hottest hours.
On weekdays during classes the campus is crowded with students, and on weekends buildings may be closed. Either way, asking in advance is the surest approach.

items.title: University Belt combination route
items.subtitle: Walking from FEU to nearby historic sites

children.text: Visit Quiapo Church or San Sebastian Church first, then have breakfast.
Tour the FEU campus. About 2 hours is enough to see the buildings and artworks.
After lunch, head to the University of Santo Tomas Historic Campus or the Manila Metropolitan Theater to compare architecture from the same era in Manila.
By taxi or Grab from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to the campus, the trip takes about
40 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic. It can take much longer during rush hours.
You can also go to an LRT station first and transfer to a train, but with luggage a taxi or Grab is more comfortable.
Recto Station on LRT-2 and Doroteo Jose Station on LRT-1 are relatively close. From the station you walk or take a jeepney or tricycle to the campus; the distance is roughly
, so check it on a map app.
The easiest way is to set "Far Eastern University, Nicanor Reyes Street" as your destination in a taxi or Grab.

City buses and jeepneys heading to northern Manila also tend to pass near the intersection of Quezon Boulevard and Recto Avenue, so it is easy to get off near the university belt. Routes change often, so ask the driver or a fellow passenger about "FEU" before boarding.
The University Belt is good for walking, but sidewalks are narrow and there are many motorcycles and cars. Be careful when crossing.

Because you will spend a long time walking around the buildings, the dry season from November to May is the most comfortable. In March–May, however, daytime temperatures are high, so visit in the morning.
The hours when the university is open and its academic calendar vary from year to year, so it is a good idea to check the semester, exam and vacation schedule beforehand.

and may vary with local conditions.

The University Belt has many cheap student restaurants and snack stalls, so lunch or a snack is easy to find. Rather than hunting for a famous shop, pick one with a line of students and you will rarely go wrong. Judge hygiene with your own eyes.

There are more lodging options in Ermita, Malate and Makati than right around FEU. If you plan to see Quiapo, Binondo and Intramuros as well, it is efficient to stay in central Manila and travel by taxi or LRT.
After lunch, a cafe in the University Belt is a good place to rest and sort your photos. The Ermita and Malate area, where many Koreans stay, is about
20–30 minutes
from the University Belt by taxi, so having dinner there is a common plan.
This is not a formal tourist attraction but a university that is still in operation. Before your visit, email FEU to ask whether you may enter and whether guided tours are available.
The gate may ask about your purpose or request ID, so bring a copy of your passport or another ID.
Keep quiet in classrooms and the library while classes are in session, and avoid taking photos that put students directly in the frame.
People may be praying in the chapel, so dress modestly and do not use a flash.
You will enjoy the visit much more if you learn each building's architect and year, and each artwork's artist, in advance. Read the highlights first before you go.
In the morning the temperature is lower and sunlight falls evenly on the building facades, which makes for better photos.
If you combine Quiapo Church and the University of Santo Tomas on the same day, there is a lot of walking, so wear comfortable shoes.
Artwork locations and the areas open to visitors can change, so check the latest announcements.
Filming with a camera and tripod may require permission, so ask about it when you inquire about a tour.
Explanatory plaques are not found everywhere. A guided tour will give you far more about the artists and buildings.
This is a university campus, not a tourist attraction, so the way visitors are admitted can change at any time. Check with the university before you leave.
There are pickpockets in the University Belt, so carry your phone and bag in front of you.
During the semester, students flood the area in front of the gate at lunchtime and it gets very crowded.
Building interiors (the auditorium and parts of the library) may be off limits without permission.
When it rains, roads in the University Belt flood easily, so leave extra time in the rainy season.
Make sure taxis use the meter; using Grab means fewer fare disputes.
Do not follow touts offering tours with no official fee. Ask the guards at the university gate or an official information desk instead.
